Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to put a few words on the record regarding Bill C-75 which I know you know, and other Members of this House know, is not a terribly well drafted piece of legislation yet, but we are working at it today, particularly in relation to amendments to Clause 4.
This clause, as the Minister's Parliamentary Secretary knows, has raised the ire of those in the vessel ownership community from one end of the country to the other. I know that Clause 4 subsection 3.1, to which my colleague, the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. Angus) is directing his Motions Nos. 5 and 6 in particular, has been negatively received by communities in my constituency, especially Prince Rupert. Whether it is the commercial fishing industry or people involved with larger vessels that come in for coal, grain, wood or anything else, they have been quite alarmed at the potential effects of subsection 3.1 and the way in which it might be implemented. I know when I spoke before that I said it was a bit of a trojan horse regulatory clause. It does not provide for the specifics of what most vessel owners would like to see in place.
I know that motions have been passed by the city councils of Prince Rupert, Kitimat and Stewart. I know there has been extensive correspondence to the committee, to the Minister and myself from the Queen Charlotte Islands and from many other areas on the North Coast from Hartley Bay, Kitkatla, Metlakatla, Oona River, Queen Charlotte City, Sandspit, Point Clements, and Masset. They have all gone on record as making sure that the Minister is aware of their concerns, particularly about the size of the cost recovery which the Minister indicated on the record some time ago was what he had in mind, it being 15 per cent of the roughly $826 million which was the calculated cost for Coast Guard services for the coming fiscal year. This meant that the Minister was trying to get something well in excess of $100 million in user-fees from vessel owners.
While this clause has gone through committee stage and has had some further potential cost recovery items added to it, for that reason before going to Motions Nos. 5, 6 and 11, which have been grouped for this afternoon, I would like to deal with the new wording of Clause 4 which would amend subsection 3.1. It says:
For the purpose of defraying the cost of services provided by the Canadian Coast Guard, the Governor in Council may make regulations respecting charges relating to those services, including, without limiting the generality of the foregoing, aids to navigation, sounding and dredging, vessel traffic services, icebreaking services and marine aid.
As I am sure Members of the House know, the words "sounding" and "marine aid" have been added. In an area of the country from where I come which represents many thousands of miles of coastline, including some of the most treacherous waters anywhere on the continent, in particular the Hecate Strait which frequently gets winds up to 100 miles an hour and where very large and very small vessels run into extreme difficulties, many large and many small boats have gone down with a great loss of life. Mariners generally, whether they go out to sail, to fish, or to operate tugboats or large vessels, are always concerned about weather changes and safety.
One of the elements of safety touched on by Clause 4 in subsection 3.1, as it is written, is that it brings in the idea of cost recovery without making it clear what the conditions are wherein cost recovery would be considered. As fishermen have pointed out to me, if you were out in a boat with waves only four feet high with winds blowing about 25 mph out of the southeast and you are trying to make a decision whether to call the Coast Guard because you know that one of your friends three months before had to put a similar call in similar wave and wind daytime conditions only to have had to pay full user-fee costs to be brought back into Prince Rupert, you would have to weigh the situation. You might wait until the waves are five feet high and you are taking on water, a couple of hundred gallons a minute, but then it might be too late.
The Canadian economy shares generally in the benefits that come from the northern B.C. coast, $500 million this past year, from the fishing industry, the export of coal, grain, wood or regular transit of tourist vessels, the B.C. ferry system and everything else that goes on in marine commerce on the West Coast. Or, as my colleague has so ably pointed out, as regards the Seaway, and our northern and eastern coasts. These kinds of things need to be responded to much more clearly by Parliament and the Minister than has been the case to date. That is why my colleague has put before us Motions Nos. 5 and 6. Those affected by the new regulatory mechanisms, everyone who owns a company, large or small, and who has something other than that which is rowed around or sailed around is seriously interested in where these regulations are going to go. Yet we do not have them. As the Speaker said earlier today, there is no schedule in this Bill as to what the regulations are going to be. It is a big unknown. It is still a Trojan horse document. Vessel owners and operators do not know what the cost is going to be. Since it is a prerogative of


the Crown to provide a precise regime within which the regulations could come forward, my colleague has put forward a way in which those affected by new regulations can go to their Member of Parliament. He or she can get in touch with 19 other Members of this House and launch a process whereby a regulation can be reviewed by a parliamentary process. There is a precise time frame within which that is to be reported back and dealt with.
Motion No. 6 goes further than that. It provides for an economic review of the impact of these user-fees on various sectors. That is a good idea, particularly when we look at what is happening in the U.S. There is legislation before the U.S. Congress to remove all Seaway fees. Here we have a Republican administration saying it does not think this idea of user-fees and licence fees and all these other things is good for commerce. Our country benefits generally from this kind of commerce so we are going to do away with the fees.
There you have the right wingers to the south of us saying that this is not the way to go. Yet here we have the Minister of Transport and his colleagues saying that they are looking for some other way to raise another $100 million or $200 million or $300 million, so we are going to have regulations. "We will not tell you what they are or how you can change them or when we are going to proclaim them, or exactly how they are going to affect you. Just, here it is, you voted for us and you are going to get it anyway."
I think Government Members should, in good conscience, vote in favour of these two motions because they provide a mechanism to protect their constituents and local economies. They provide for a very important process whereby a badly drafted Bill such as this one can have some of its negative or positive aspects reviewed by the House. I think that makes good sense.
I see you are indicating that I am running out of time. That is too bad because I know my constituents are very much interested in seeing this Bill changed, in particular Clause 4. It tends to go after those who should not be subject to these kinds of costs. I am thinking again of those in the fishing industry running very close to the line. As we learned today, this Government does not intend to do anything about an inappropriate countervailing duty brought against all our fishermen on the East Coast. That duty will mean a couple of million dollars out of their pockets. Many of our coastal industries, the fishing industry and many of our commercial trades, are very close to the point of just breaking even. Many of these user-fees require very close scrutiny by this House. That is why I think these motions should be supported. I trust you will be voting the right way, Mr. Speaker, later today.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe):
subtopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there should be no question here today until such time as Members have had an opportunity to discuss this Bill thoroughly. I know that Members, deep down, are concerned about the impact of Bill C-75. About 99 per cent of the representations the legislative committee heard concerned Clause 4. That is true regardless of where the representations came from, whether it be the Canadian Boating Association in Ontario or British Columbia, or fishermen in Atlantic Canada and British Columbia. What they were most concerned about was that this clause gives the Government the power to impose user-fees on various boat owners. It does not matter whether they run great ships through the Great Lakes or paddle a canoe in an acid-filled lake in Ontario.
The great frustration for all those who came before the legislative committee, and the great frustration for every right thinking Member of the House of Commons about Clause 4, is that even though the Bill gives the Minister the power to impose charges for what was provided as a service by the Government, he has not defined who or how much he is going to charge. Is he going to charge 1 per cent of the cost of providing a service or is he going to charge 100 per cent? I suppose, at least in theory, the Minister could impose a charge equal to 150 per cent of the cost of providing a service. He could make money on the deal. He could make it a commercial operation under Clause 4.
The Government is asking Members of Parliament to pass a Bill which will allow the Minister to impose charges on Canadians without giving us any idea whatsoever how they are to be imposed. A fishermen in a community in P.E.I. is looking at a loaded gun with the trigger pull being passed to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski). He does not know whether the Minister is going to fire a warning shot, put one across his bow, or blow his head off. He has no idea whether a little bit of buckshot is to be sprinkled on the tail end of the boat, hitting a few lobster pots, or whether it is going to send him to the bottom. The Minister demands and will receive, if the majority responds in the normal way, the authority to impose these charges. We are not to be told how that gun is to be used. That is simply unacceptable. I ask Members to reach down inside themselves and question their conscience, their sense of democracy, their sense of the right of the individual in this country, and reject this archaic legislation, which of course is not deserving of consideration by intelligent men and women of conscience in this Chamber.

Designation of Nova Scotia

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   THE OFFICIAL DESIGNATION OF NOVA SCOTIA ACT MEASURE TO ENACT

speechtext: The House resumed from Friday, November 30, 1984, consideration of the motion of Mr. Nowlan that Bill C-201, an Act respecting the official designation of "Nova Scotia", be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   THE OFFICIAL DESIGNATION OF NOVA SCOTIA ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on Bill C-201, an Act representing the official designation of Nova Scotia. I want to express the gratitude of the House to the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan) for presenting this Bill, which obviously is important to him as a Nova Scotian.
This Bill's thrust is as follows: In every place where the words "Nova Scotia" appear in any Act, regulation, statutory instrument, report, contract, lease, licence or other document the proper designation of this name in both official languages is and shall be "Nova Scotia".
The purpose of this Bill is to retain the Latin title "Nova Scotia" for official purposes, in both English and French documents. This would mean, more specifically, that the designation "Nouvelle-Ecosse" would be changed to the Latin, "Nova Scotia".
These issues, especially where proper names are in question, can lead to emotional debate, and in my view these kinds of questions should be considered very seriously before decisions are taken on them.
There are also other very serious points of a constitutional nature which should be made with respect to this Bill. To begin with, as worded this Bill would apply to any report, contract, lease, licence or other document. However, by Section 92(13) of the Constitution Act, 1867, jurisdiction over property and civil rights in the province belongs to the province, and to this extent the legislation would be subject to constitutional challenge. I wonder if it is the intention of the legislation to require, for example, that the Bank of Nova Scotia, which is well known in French as La Banque de Nouvelle-Ecosse change its French letterhead in writing to French clients. Indeed, if it could not use the French name in written documents, would it necessarily follow as a business matter if nothing else, that it would also need to change any signs on its building?
According to the Official Languages Act and the Constitution Act, 1982, both versions of Acts of Parliament in the official languages of Canada are equally authentic. It happens that the name "Nova Scotia", and its French version "Nouvelle-Ecosse", appear in some 40 federal statutes, including the Supreme Court Act, the Judges Act, and the Interpretation
Act. The French version "Nouvelle-Ecosse" also appears, of course, in other jurisprudence.
It appears that for at least 270 years "Nouvelle-Ecosse" has been the accepted French term to describe Nova Scotia. Encyclopaedias, text books, dictionaries, atlases, journals, periodicals, newspapers, et cetera, throughout the Frenchspeaking world have used and are using that expression as a matter of course, and nowhere is there any indication that there might be some doubt about its propriety.
You may agree, therefore, that we are dealing here with an issue that goes much beyond legal technicalities and that it is surprising to discover that a time-honoured expression such as "Nouvelle-Ecosse", which is solidly enshrined in a language as universal as French, should be questioned on grounds, allegedly, that there might not be a proper basis for it. It might be noted that common usage, when it comes to names of countries, places, et cetera, is recognized in Section 30 of the Interpretation Act.
In any event, "Nouvelle-Ecosse" was used to describe this area by France and Britain, the two successive sovereign authorities originally there, in the official French version of the Treaty of Utrecht, 1713. It would seem to me that several centuries of use give legitimacy to the words "Nouvelle-Ecosse".

speakeroldname: Mr. Gordon Towers (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   THE OFFICIAL DESIGNATION OF NOVA SCOTIA ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have known the Hon. Member from Nova Scotia a long time. In fact, he was a Member when I first came to the House of Commons almost 14 years ago. One of the things that I have always recognized is the dedication and the sincerity of the Hon. Member. Certainly he has been a very stalwart Member of Parliament, as well as a very imaginative one. He has made a tremendous contribution, not only to this House of Commons, but to Canada generally.
There is no doubt in my mind that in proposing this Bill he did it as a dedicated Canadian. He did it as he felt it was something he thought should be done, especially coming as he does from that province. Anything that we have to say is in support of his dedication.
When we look back at the debate which took place on this Bill on March 27, 1981 when it was a Bill called Bill C-217,1 must admit that I found interesting the various points of research which the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan) presented at that time in support of his motion. That speech was really a mini-history lesson outlining as it did the origins of words like Quebec, Ontario and Canada. My earliest recollection of Canadian history was the native word for Canada which was "Kanata". No doubt that is one of the reasons we have a small community near Ottawa today that is called Kanata.
Without doubt, many Canadian words have their origins in various languages. Native Indian or Inuit words, for instance,


are very prevalent in place names. This is logical, taking into account the historical development of our country, and taking into account, first of all, the native population that was here when the early explorers found this part of the world. We had people from many nations that found their way to our country. I think one of the earliest stages of history found the North American continent divided, north and south, between the Portuguese and the Spanish. Then as history progressed, changes took place. Then there became a division on the 49th parallel. There have been many changes made, and each individual who came to this country brought with him a part of his own homeland, a heartland that he really appreciated.
For instance, there is Kananaskis, which is very much on the map now as far as Alberta is concerned, there is Lac la Biche, and then take the other word, "cafe". I have heard people from south of the border call it "cafee", and then, of course, others call it restaurant. There are many interpretations of different words that we have in our language.
Few Canadian place names can boast of a Latin origin, but Nova Scotia is one of them. In English that Latin designation has remained rather than being translated into "New Scotland". In French, "Nouvelle-Ecosse" was chosen as the name for Nova Scotia. Apparently, "Nouvelle-Ecosse" has been the accepted French terminology for at least 273 years. That is a long time in Canadian history. It is described as "Nouvelle-Ecosse" in the official French version of the Treaty of Utrecht of 1713. I do not know how many Members are aware that Utrecht is in Holland. One of my earlier relations came from that part of the world. This is no recent development. We are looking back at the very roots of Nova Scotia-aux vraies racines de la Nouvelle-Ecosse.
Place names become dear to our heart. It may be that Francophones, who over the years have known Nouvelle-Ecosse as either their province of origin, or as a splendid Canadian province that they would like to visit, cannot easily change their habits and suddently think of Nova Scotia. I wonder if there is any solid reason for doing so? Nowadays, Nova Scotia is commonly regarded not as a Latin name but as the English version of the Province's name. Surely Francophones would prefer a title which is clearly French and which has been so through the centuries.
I know that the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants has gone to great pains to point out that the motivation for his Bill has nothing to do with the bilingual question but that it has to do with the importance of using proper names for places in this country: "The proper use of proper nouns", as the Hon. Member put it. At the outset I tried to make the point that the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants is very sincere in what he is doing and what he is proposing. I am sure that many Hon. Members feel that "Nouvelle-Ecosse", a designation in use for close to three centuries, is indeed the proper use of a proper noun.
Designation of Nova Scotia
The Hon. Member for Annpolis Valley-Hants has stated on occasion that he would like to see the name changed in terms of tourism. Surely, saying: " Venez en Nouvelle-Ecosse" can be as great a spur to tourism as: " Venez en Nova Scotia".
Think of all the maps that would need to be redrawn, all the legislation which would need to be redrafted, all the signs which would need to be repainted if the name of the province were changed. Perhaps one of the weaknesses of the Bill is that the Hon. Member has not thought about the problems that it would create.
I am not opposed to change just for the sake of opposing change. I have always believed that I am a person who always looks to the future with optimism. However, we know that there are many reasons for changing place names. Istanbul versus Constantinople reflects a change in political power. Tanzania versus Zanzibar and Tanganyika reflects a change in geographic boundaries. Members of the House will be aware that even the names of our constituencies change from time to time as a result of the change in boundaries.
Pearson International Airport as opposed to Toronto International Airport reflects a means of paying honour to a respected statesman. Many changes are made from time to time for special reasons, but those reasons must be sound and reasonable.
There are all kinds of reasons for changing place names. In order for the change to stand the test of time, there has to be compelling logic behind it, because Canadians are logical people who want to know why changes are made.
In the present case, I can think of no reason so compelling that it would cause me to unseat the present nomenclature of "Nouvelle Ecosse" for another name.
I am grateful for this opportunity to speak on a very important matter to the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley- Hants. I am pleased that we are able to express our own concerns and feelings in Private Members' Hour.

Mr. Speaker, I want to make a short intervention with regard to the Bill put forward by the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan). Personally, I have mixed feelings about this Bill. I understand the Hon. Member's desire to assert what he believes very strongly is the name of his home province.
I am reminded of my childhood, growing up in English Canada, and being told of a place along the St. Lawrence River called Three Rivers. Over time, with the change in official documents and the usage of the name, that community reverted to its original French name of Trois Rivieres. Similarly, I believe the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley- Hants is attempting to provide for the recognition that Nova Scotia, or New Scotland, is a name that reflects its Scottish heritage and should be recognized as such.
Having said that, I am not sure that we in the House of Commons are the ones who should initiate that kind of change. I would be very reluctant to do so unless we had a very definite


Designation of Nova Scotia
resolution passed by the Legislature of the Province of Nova Scotia indicating that there is the collective desire for such a change. At that time, perhaps with a petition from Members of Parliament from that province, the House could give further consideration to the Bill brought forward by the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants. However, I also have no objection to this Bill going to a committee of the House for further consideration.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   THE OFFICIAL DESIGNATION OF NOVA SCOTIA ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can't help thinking Bill C-201 is rather confusing, if we read the French title of the Bill: "Loi concernant le nom officielle de la "Nouvelle-Ecosse"", and then realize that the designation "Nouvelle-Ecosse" is being challenged by this Bill.
"Nouvelle-Ecosse" is a designation hallowed by a 300-year old tradition, as was already pointed out. It is the name we find in the Treaty of Utrecht, under which France ceded Nova Scotia to Great Britain in 1713. The region belonged to the French from 1667 to 1710. Originally called "Acadie", it was known as "Nouvelle-Ecosse" in the early 1700's. Mr. Speaker, personally I would hesitate, and so should all Members of this House, to reverse this historic tradition.
The French designation for this part of the country has been "Nouvelle-Ecosse" in all Canada's official documents, including documents of a constitutional nature.
As Hon. Members are well aware, the Constitution is a document that applies both to the provinces and to the federal Government. I do not think the federal Government can unilaterally change the official title of a province without obtaining prior consent from that province.
I don't think we have any reason to believe that there is a vast movement of support in Nova Scotia for this Bill. It seems that Nova Scotia's Francophones are quite satisfied with the name of their province. Substituting Nova Scotia, now considered more as an English than a Latin designation, for Nouvelle-Ecosse, would be of no benefit to Nova Scotians of French origin.
I also think that a particularly compelling argument is provided by toponymy or the study of place names. In toponymy, current and past usage is one of the main elements to be considered.
The Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan) emphasized that he was in favour of the Latin designation, not conformity with English usage.
With all due respect for Latin and its vital contribution to our civilization and even to both our official languages, there is nothing in Canada today that really obliges us, either historically or traditionally, to give precedence to the Latin version. The designation "Nova Scotia" is no longer considered a Latin term. Over time and in common usage, it has acquired an English connotation for the purposes of geographic designation.
Mr. Speaker, I think we should act prudently and without undue haste, since we lack a consensus reflecting all the views of the various groups in our society. I also have some hesitation in agreeing such a measure would be both practical and justified.

speakeroldname: Mr. Girve Fretz (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Mines)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Mines)
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   THE OFFICIAL DESIGNATION OF NOVA SCOTIA ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find very interesting the arguments of the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan) for introducing this Bill which would supplant "Nouvelle-Ecosse" with "Nova Scotia". According to the Hon. Member, the name "Nova Scotia", because it is Latin, should not be translated because in translation it loses its status as a proper name.
When we travel abroad, we travel to Venice, not to Venezia. We go to Florence, not Fiorenze, and to Rome, not Roma. In our English and French usage, we have not hesitated to change the names used in various countries, adapting them to our own linguistic milieu. Similarly, there is nothing sacrosanct about the Latin words "Nova Scotia". In English we could have changed that to "New Scotland". But that did not happen, and over the years the fact that "Nova Scotia" was Latin became more or less submerged by the fact that "Nova Scotia" was the English designation for a Canadian province, otherwise known as "Nouvelle-Ecosse" in the other major language of Canada.
This is an historical fact. There is nothing peculiar about it. There is no law that says English and French must evolve in exactly the same way. Indeed such a premise would be an antithesis to all these persons who view the properties of our two official languages as being unique and unbridled. In short, just because English Canadians did not change "Nova Scotia" to "New Scotland" is no reason for French Canadians not to have changed the name to "Nouvelle-Ecosse". To seek linguistic conformity in regard to vocabulary would be an affront to both our official languages.
I wonder if the Hon. Member has considered all the changes which would be necessary if this Bill were passed. My colleague who spoke before me has already referred to changes in maps, legislation and signs which would be required to reflect the new reality. Changes would go far beyond matters of federal jurisdiction. Every town and hamlet in Nova Scotia would be affected. And while there might not be a wholesale rush to change the letterheads of companies, name plates on buildings and tourist maps and other written materials about the province, there would be a certain confusion about the whole situation. One could even envisage factions arising; one faction saying: "Leave the maps and name plates alone" and the other saying: "No, we must reflect what has been legislated."
Every benefit must be weighed against possible disadvantages. If the disadvantages are weightier than the benefit, then it is very much to be questioned if there is, in fact, a benefit.


This is a situation of that type. If indeed it is a benefit to have purity of form in respecting Latin, then let us weigh that against the factors of the effect on the population and the cost.
If this Bill were to lead to great happiness in the province by those persons affected by the change, I would favour moving ahead quickly with this Bill. However, I must admit that I can see no striking advantages.
I would like to add another factor for consideration, that of the image abroad. More persons than ever are travelling to Canada these days because of Expo and what is happening overseas, and we can assume that many of them will want to travel to our beautiful seaside province known in all Francophone tourist literature as "Nouvelle-Ecosse". Who is to explain to all these hordes of would-be tourists that, alas, Nouvelle-Ecosse is no more? What will Francophone tourists think of a province which has just lost its clearly French appelation? How will they interpret that, I wonder? Would they be disappointed or upset by this change? I think that would be unfortunate, Mr. Speaker.
Nova Scotia, with its Acadian culture and its growing number of Francophone institutions is proudly Francophone, just as it is proudly Anglohone. Both parts of that collectivity deserve the right to express themselevs in the name which they have chosen historically and to which they have cleaved over the centuries, Nova Scotia in English, Nouvelle-Ecosse in French.
I also wonder what has happened to the Official Opposition. We do not have one member of the Liberal Party in the House of Commons, not merely to contribute to the debate, but there are none here at all. Thank you and merci, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   THE OFFICIAL DESIGNATION OF NOVA SCOTIA ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my name is Carole Jacques, Member for Montreal-Mercier. Mr. Speaker, a lawyer's memory never fails, they say.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to speak to the Bill entitled An Act respecting the official designation of "Nova Scotia" . I want to approach this matter from a national angle.
One might say that the name "Nova Scotia" is part of the cultural heritage of Nova Scotians and, in fact, of all Canadians. It is a part of our cultural heritage because it is the name which for nearly 300 years has appeared in all our official documents, all our newspapers, all our business or personal correspondence.
How would a Francophone used to saying "Je viens de la Nouvelle-Ecosse" feel if, henceforth, he had to say "Je viens de la Nova Scotia"? Probably the same way an Anglophone would feel when saying "I come from Nouvelle-Ecosse". One would get the impression the sentence was begun in one language and finished in the other.
The words "Nova Scotia" may very well be derived from Latin, but still they do sound English because they have been used for years to designate one of our maritime provinces. It would be too much to ask Francophones to say "Nova Scotia"
Designation of Nova Scotia
instead of "Nouvelle-Ecosse", just at it would be to ask Anglophones to substitute the words "Colombie-Britannique" for the words "British Columbia". In either case it would be foreign to the speaker's language.
Is there any logic in the fact that Anglophones did not translate the latin phrase Nova Scotia, as Francophones did? Rather than logic, what is involved is a historical process that led to the constant use of the words Nova Scotia on one side, and Nouvelle-Ecosse on the other. I feel it is not proper that we should be logical to the point of imposing uniformity in all areas.
Canada was not built on uniformity. The proof is that we have here today French-speaking Members and Englishspeaking Members. What gives this country its character is that it was developed under the influence of various stimuli, each evolving in its own right. Let us not now impose rigid uniformity.
Mr. Speaker, when I was a child, I had the chance to visit Nova Scotia, and its people with their extraordinarily warm hospitality that is well reflected in the words Nouvelle-Ecosse. It would be infringing upon their rights if we were to substitute the latin name Nova Scotia. The rights of citizens secured over centuries, contrary to toponymic usage, would require amendments to constitutional documents-and besides, this is a provincial matter-and a number of necessary changes dealt with by federal law, and soon and so forth, Mr. Speaker. This would have a negative impact on the French-speaking population, because Nova Scotia is perceived as an English name.
The translation of names goes contrary to good usage with respect to proper names. The name is Latin and not English. The name is to be found in the 1621 Charter issued by King James to William Alexander. We must realize, Mr. Speaker, that Nova Scotia has very dynamic minorities which have vested rights over time that we cannot infringe upon. We have to respect as a Government and as a federal Parliament the rights of the French-language minorities outside Quebec.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   THE OFFICIAL DESIGNATION OF NOVA SCOTIA ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 welcome this opportunity today to see our Anglophone Members in the House of Commons vehemently defending a French designation whose existence has been consecrated by history! I am very proud of my Anglophone colleagues today.
I am proud of my Anglophone colleagues who are defending so vigorously the French appellation "Nouvelle-Ecosse". This is an historic moment, not only in the House of Commons, but in the Progressive Conservative Party, which was once


Designation of Nova Scotia
renowned as an English-speaking Party. Today, we have direct proof to the contrary.

To get back to the debate, Mr. Speaker, some examples were given earlier of foreign designations of certain cities famous for their culture, such as the French "Venise" and the English "Venice" for the Italian "Venezia", and for centuries no one has objected to the different names in other languages. Even London, which is called "Londres" in French and London of course in English. There is Greece and the magnificent island of Corfu, Kerkyra, and here again there has been no objection to these different designations through the ages.
Mr. Speaker, the name "Nouvelle-Ecosse" has been hallowed by history and by the suffering of a people that deserves all our support and admiration, and I am referring to the Acadians.
It is probably the only vestige Acadians have retained of their country of origin, and I am referring to this very direct and very French designation, "Nouvelle-Ecosse", which was immediately accepted by all Anglophones in the surrounding area, even in Prince Edward Island.
I wonder what will happen if we have to change the name of a province. What all those lawyers are going to think up-some would say there are too many of them here in the House-what are all those lawyers going to say when the door has been opened by legal precedent? Will they dare change British Columbia to Canadian Columbia? Will they ask to change "Nouveau-Brunswick" to New Brunswick or Nouvelle-Allemagne? Where will that open door lead us?
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I respectfully submit to the House that the designation "Nova Scotia" was adapted and adopted by the English because of its cultural flavour, the ability to speak Latin then being the "in" thing in some European courts. That's the reason why the English had adopted it. It is clear, however, that if they had wanted to call it "New Scotland", they would have done so as they did for New Brunswick. I think that the designation "Nouvelle-Ecosse" is a time-honoured one which should be preserved jealously not only for the local people, but also for the people in Western Canada, in Ontario, as well as in Quebec who have always known our Canadian provinces by their own names. And the designation "Nouvelle-Ecosse" suits perfectly the fine province of Nova Scotia. I suggest, therefore, that we should keep it.
Second, I feel that this is not the proper forum to discuss such an issue, Mr. Speaker. I suggest it is the fact of a very old Government to say that we are going to send instructions to the provinces. The previous Government, missed by a small minority of Canadians, had the despicable habit of sending edicts to the provinces and to tell them: That is what you are going to do. We, from the province of Quebec, know it, because we were imposed similar things with the last Constitution. This Government, however, will respect the basic rights of the
provinces and we sincerely believe that, strictly speaking, it is up to the provinces to discuss at least their name.
I think, therefore, that we should first of all refer the matter to the province of Nova Scotia before coming up with this instruction to be imposed to an individual Canadian province.
Third, Mr. Speaker, we must realize that on all maps throughout the world, the designation "Nouvelle-Ecosse" appears. In my career, I have had the opportunity to work for Zaire, a Francophone country in Africa. And I have seen in that and other countries maps of the world showing Canada with its provinces where the names "Nouvelle-Ecosse" and "Nouveau-Brunswick" appeared. These people were aware that they had French maps of the world and that French is a universal language.
By the way, if we are to make or propose changes, I dare say that we should suggest in good French the expression "adjoint parlementaire" to replace "secretaire parlementaire". It would be a very good French designation which is used in Geneva, Paris and Quebec City. I think that the expression "secretaire parlementaire" is an anglicism which we shall have to rectify one of these days.
But that is not the issue now before us, the debate is rather concerned with a name change for a province that has not yet made an official request-even though it does not have to ask- and has not yet expressed any wish to have its name changed.
Therefore, I would like to suggest to the House that this would imply a number of changes, the updating of all world maps, charts, even radio systems, navigational systems that use the phrase Nouvelle-Ecosse in French.
Fourthly, it goes without saying that to our proud French Canadians who are struggling in that beautiful country that was Acadia and has been Nova Scotia for a few centuries now, we must not give the impression that they are being deserted. As representatives of all Canada, we must support the remnants of French culture that may remain in difficult areas of Canada. French Canadians who are a very small minority in those areas of Nova Scotia should not be made to feel they are being shelved for good by that change in the name of their own province.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we should respect the vested, innate rights of our French-Canadians in Nova Scotia, who have always been proud French-Canadians and who come to visit us in Montreal once in a while, to show that the French spirit is still around, even among them.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, to sum up, I would like to bring to the attention of all Canadians today the fact that this Bill is being put forth, perhaps seriously, by people whom I shall not name but, as I must tell you, Mr. Speaker, who are now absent from the House.
Therefore, I humbly move, Mr. Speaker, that the name Nouvelle-Ecosse be and remain historically applicable to that province known in English as "the Province of Nova Scotia".

speakeroldname: Mr. Geoff Scott (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   THE OFFICIAL DESIGNATION OF NOVA SCOTIA ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
The Canadian Permanent Committee on Geographic Names, the CPCGN, has for many years held the principle that, aside from entities that come under federal jurisdiction, such as Indian reserves, national parks and military bases, geographical names fall under provincial jurisdiction. The name of a province is of course another problem altogether. According to the Department of Justice, the name of a province is the name appearing in the Act under which the province entered Confederation. In the case of Nova Scotia, this was the British North America Act. Since these are constitutional documents, the federal Government cannot proceed with any changes without having such changes ratified by the provinces. Furthermore, the provinces cannot change their names without requesting the approval of the federal Government. I think we can conclude this is an area of shared jurisdiction, where it would be up to the provincial Parliament to take the initiative.
Mr. Speaker, in toponymy, current and past usage is one of the main elements to be taken into consideration. The name "Nouvelle- Ecosse" as used on maps, in treaties, in historical works and in geographic documents goes back to the eighteenth century at least. Its use has been maintained without interruption since that time, and the name remains in common usage, not only among French-speaking Nova Scotians and all French-speaking Canadians but also throughout the Frenchspeaking world. It is the name we find in the Treaty of Utrecht of 1713, under which France formally ceded Nova Scotia to Great Britain.
We must remember that, initially colonized by France under the name "Acadie", Nova Scotia was French from 1667 to 1710. Furthermore, even if the name Nova Scotia is of Latin origin, it has been a very long time since it was perceived as such by the population of that province and Canadians in general, who consider it to be the English name of a province with a strong English-speaking majority.


Designation of Nova Scotia
Perhaps it is nothing more than a formality-important though it may be-but we must not forget either that if we were to change the official name "Nouvelle-Ecosse" we would have to change not only all federal statutes but also all official documents, maps and what have you where the provincial name appears.
The name "Nouvelle-Ecosse" is part of the cultural heritage of Nova Scotians and of all other Canadians.
On the other hand, such a change now that the attitude of most Canadians concerning bilingualism is one of greater tolerance and wider acceptance might very well stiffen relations between the two linguistic communities and polarize their respective position.
This Bill would require many changes, modifications, maps, treaties, and federal laws. As we have already said, basically it is within provincial jurisdiction. I become a little nervous about the federal Government trying to pass any kind of law without the full consultation of the province and its people, especially when the law lies within provincial jurisdiction. I am even more concerned about the negative aspect of this Bill on the Francophone population.
Nova Scotia is considered an English name. Nouvelle-Ecosse fits in truly with the bilingual character of this great country of ours and of the magnificent Province of Nova Scotia.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre Blais (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   THE OFFICIAL DESIGNATION OF NOVA SCOTIA ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak to this Bill this afternoon. I noticed that the various speakers were in a seldom seen unanimous mood and shared a common view. I think there is much similarity in the considerations which prompted us to rise.
I have always been very sensitive whenever linguistic questions arise here in Canada, particularly in Quebec where I come from and where this has always been a prominent issue. I live in an ancestral house which has been passed on from fathers to sons since 1665, over 300 years, so I do not really know whether this tradition explains why I always find it difficult to accept changes to things which are so deeply rooted in our heritage, be it in Quebec or elsewhere in Canada. I have very specific views on what constitutes our national heritage, and I think these are things that are very difficult to change. Changing a name or an expression would not really change what we want to change in this country, whatever that may be.
Take my name, for instance. It evolved in three different ways over 300 years. We never moved away, we never moved off our land, we never budged as much as three feet in 300 years, and in spite of all this, the name Blais managed to evolve and change three times. This is just an example.
However, we never had to come before Parliament to make that change. Lucky for us!
I was listening to the other speeches earlier, and I was thinking of the wealth of wonderful names we have here in Canada, including the names of our provinces and the names of our towns and villages. I was thinking, in Quebec, how much the Indian languages have given us in the form of names that are practically impossible to translate and that we would never even think of changing. For instance, the names of Quebec City, Peribonka, and Ottawa. These are all Indian names, and I feel I should name some of them to show how wonderful they are. For instance, Bellechasse, the riding I represent. We can't translate names like that. Some of my colleagues have tried to, but not very successfully. Take Sherbrooke. You could hardly translate that. I don't know in what language it would work, but you can't translate it. La Salle and Westmount. I don't know how the Hon. Member who just left us ... I don't want to bore you, but if we referred to the Hon. Member from "La montagne de l'Ouest", we might get mixed up with Members from other parts of Canada. It cannot be done.
I think we should keep the names we have in Canada. The evolution has to be natural. A moment ago I gave examples concerning my own situation.
The key question which made me think is this: How can we as a federal Government take over a provincial responsibility? In my opinion, the question is quite clear. It is not up to us to take this kind of initiative. The province itself should have expressed interest, but such is not the case. Otherwise we could seriously consider whether it is the common will of most residents of the province and what would be the reaction of other people throughout Canada.
We often hear various comments, and time and time again Governments are blamed for reacting instead of acting, which may be true in some cases. It may be true, but perhaps it is in cases such as this one where we must ask whether it is the proper way for a Government to proceed. If a Government goes too far ahead or wants to proceed too quickly to make certain changes which might antagonize people and lead to negative reactions on their part, I would suggest we have our work cut out for us if we as parliamentary legislators want to push ahead with this kind of legislative measure when we do not have an obvious consensus, either provincial or national.
Speaking sometimes in French and sometimes in English, my colleague the Hon. Member for Hamilton-Wentworth (Mr. Scott), stealing my lines, dealt with the cost of the changes. Again, at a time when each cent and each dollar in Canada counts, where we have to borrow one third-nearly 33 cents-out of every dollar we spend, we would have to borrow a lot more to make the necessary changes in legislations, regulations, maps and treaties.
Mr. Speaker, it is never interesting to have to rise to oppose such a proposal, but I think that we ought to do it and do it simply. Mr. Speaker, I feel that we have no other alternative


than to oppose this initiative, to maintain the status quo and to keep the name as it is now.
I have the feeling that you want me to conclude. I have a lot more to say, Mr. Speaker, but I will continue another time.

Mr. Speaker, as you know, my constituency of York East is made up of a portion of two of the six cities that compose the municipality of Metropolitan Toronto. My constituency is composed of a portion of the borough of East York and another portion of the municipality, the City of North York. My municipality and constituency have a very multicultural population. In my constituency there reside over 60 different ethnic and cultural groups all together.
I had the privilege of serving as the Mayor of my municipality, the borough of East York, for a number of years. While serving in that capacity, we established a multicultural committee in East York. It later became the race relations multicultural committee of East York. A short time later, the City of North York established a similar type of committee. It is known as the Mayor's Race Relations Committee for the City of North York. We have a friendly rivalry in our two municipalities, Mr. Speaker, as to which one of these organizations was actually the first of its kind.
The East York Multicultural Committee was originally created for two purposes. One was to allow all of our residents, no matter from which cultural background they came or for how long they had lived in our community, to get to know and
Adjournment Debate
to understand one another better and, at the same time, to encourage the members of our community, whether newcomers or long time residents, to become involved and participate in the wider community activities and life.
The North York committee, on the other hand, was created to deal specifically with race relations matters. It grew out of incidents in Metropolitan Toronto in the late 1970s when race relations, relationships with the police, and relationships in various communities were of great concern. As a result of that, the focus and the main attention of that committee was placed on the race relations aspect.
I do not think it really matters which one of those committees was first. Both are geared toward promotion of good relationships in our community, whether race relations or the whole relationship of getting people to know and understand each other better. On top of those two functions, however, both committees are geared to ensure that all people have the opportunity to participate and become involved in the wider community. That is what multiculturalism is all about, in my view.
The Sunday before last in my municipality, the borough of East York, we had our great multicultural festival which is known as East York Day. On the platform that day we had two people who exemplified what multiculturalism is all about. One was the new Lieutenant-Governor of the Province of Ontario, His Honour, Lincoln Alexander. He is the first black Canadian to serve as Lieutenant-Governor of a province. He was born in this country, in the City of Toronto. In order to take his full place in the wider Canadian society, he had to overcome great problems and obstacles. Another man on the platform that day was the Chairman of East York Day, a man by the name of Shamoh Kara. He came here as a refugee from Tanzania many years ago. He has become prominent in his own community and in the wider community.
Those are two great examples of what multiculturalism is all about. Our community is committed to multiculturalism, and so is our Government. It is moving beyond traditional multiculturalism into equality of economic opportunity. It has been doing that in two areas recently. One is the employment equity Bill which has just gone into committee. The other is an initiative which the Minister of State for Multiculturalism (Mr. Jelinek) recently took in Toronto through a conference called Multiculturalism Means Business. At that conference, and also in the debate concerning employment equity, one thing became quite clear: The concern of many of our fellow Canadians is about the question of whether or not there is discrimination, whether it be in employment or in business.
On April 14 I put a question to the Minister of State for Multiculturalism and asked him if the new multiculturalism business centre which he proposed at the conference was going to deal with this issue. I asked him that specifically, bearing in mind the concern people have over the enforcement of the rules and regulations set out in the employment equity Bill,


Adjournment Debate
and the concerns people have about enforcing equality of opportunity and anti-discriminatory measures in business itself. I hope that tonight the Parliamentary Secretary is going to tell us that not only will this business centre deal with those matters but tell us specifically how, and tell us about the enforcement provisions which are needed to overcome discrimination in these areas.

speakeroldname: Mr. Vincent Della Noce (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Minister of State (Multiculturalism)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport); Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Multiculturalism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take this opportunity to reply to the question of my colleague from York East (Mr. Redway). I am pleased to be able to speak to this matter which is important to all of us-equality of opportunity. This is what our Government stands for and the purpose of our multiculturalism policies and programs.
Of course, we are talking about equality in all aspects of Canadian life: equality of cultural opportunity, equality of social opportunity, and equality of political opportunity. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer to the remarks of our Minister at the Toronto Convention Centre on April 11,
1986.	He said, and I quote:
When I speak of equality, I mean all aspects of life in Canadian society:
Cultural equality-to preserve, encourage and promote the cultures, practices and customs which are the very essence of a truly multicultural society;
Social equality-to respect the right of every individual to take part freely in the life of society without coming up against the constraints imposed by racism, intolerance and fanaticism;
Political equality-to give everyone the opportunity to take part in the decisions made in municipal, provincial and federal affairs.
Mr. Speaker, needless to say, those are my own priorities, and I am quoting the Minister, and they are also those of the Government of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, at the same time, our Government continues to support cultural retention and enhancement, as well as the greater integration of Canadian society, both through individual learning or skills acquisition and through the evolution of institutions to reflect and be open to Canadians of all cultures and races.
Such an open society is attractive to investors and entrepreneurial immigrants from countries around the world. They can feel welcome here and feel that their children will have equal opportunities for advancement. At the same time, such a society is open to a more effective use of all its human talents and resources.
The recent Multiculturalism Means Business conference is an example of initiative that promotes equality of economic opportunity. The conference brought together about 700 people from across the country from many ethnocultural backgrounds, representing all levels of Governments; community organizations; individual businesses of all sizes; business,
trade and professional associations. Many doors of opportunity were opened and many contacts were made.
The momentum generated by this conference will be continued and the issues raised there will be addressed. A multiculturalism and business centre is one initiative to increase economic opportunity for all Canadians, both in terms of business and employment opportunity.
The Government's commitment has not waned on social and cultural issues. The Government has already announced its commitment to the second decade to combat racism and racial discrimination. At the same time, the Minister of State for Multiculturalism (Mr. Jelinek) released the progress report on Equality Now recommendations.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I would like to reiterate this Government's commitment to a society where all Canadians enjoy equality of opportunity in all spheres of life, social, cultural, political and economical. Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: WESTERN GRAIN STABILIZATION ACT-SIZE OF PAYMENT TO FARMERS. (B) REQUEST FOR ANNOUNCEMENT OF DEFICIENCY PAYMENTS
WESTERN GRAIN STABILIZATION ACT-SIZE OF PAYMENT TO FARMERS. (B) REQUEST FOR ANNOUNCEMENT OF DEFICIENCY PAYMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government has a responsibility to deal with the crisis in farm income, particularly in the grain producing sector. The extraordinary drops in income, caused partially by the EEC and U.S. action in the market, merits extraordinary response from the Government. Members of this House and many farm organizations have been asking, since the initial grain price announcements, for some indication that the Government intends to live up to its commitment to take some action.
The western grain stabilization payments of $600 are timely and appreciated, but they are also a very good indicator of the magnitude of the income reduction that has been taking place. The western grain stabilization makes up for income shortfalls for 1985-86. It does not deal with the projected shortfall or income reduction in the 1986-87 crop year. That shortfall, with $3 wheat indicated by the initial payment announcement, will be $1 billion. In fact, the Saskatchewan Pool Research Branch has indicated that it feels that, with all areas and grains included, it is likely to be a shortfall closer to $2 billion. The western grain stabilization plan may trigger another payout in 1986-87, but by its very nature it eats itself. Each time a pay-out is triggered, it indicates a lower income, which lowers the five-year average. Therefore, the next pay-outs are going to be progressively smaller, particularly if the pay-out is triggered in successive years.
The grain producing community is asking the Government to make a commitment to ensure that the incomes of farmers next year will at least be equal to 1985-86. If that is not done, there will be far fewer farmers to help in 1987. I hope the strategy of the Government is not to reduce the number of farms and eliminate a number of farmers so that the need for assistance will be less, as has been suggested by others, and implied in the Nielsen report.


I hope the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) will announce in his press conference tomorrow programs such as are available to United States and European farmers. Such programs would solve the problems for many farmers by assuring at least the cost of production in deficiency payments. As I said earlier, extraordinary drops in farm income demand extraordinary action. We would appreciate an indication of the Government's action now.

speakeroldname: Hon. Charles Mayer (Minister of State (Canadian Wheat Board)):
subtopic: WESTERN GRAIN STABILIZATION ACT-SIZE OF PAYMENT TO FARMERS. (B) REQUEST FOR ANNOUNCEMENT OF DEFICIENCY PAYMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo) raises a concern that is felt by all of us connected with agriculture in Canada. I should point out that it is not only an issue affecting western Canada-which many people have come to believe is the grain growing area of Canada-it also affects the total Canadian agricultural picture.
When we consider the amount of grain produced in various provinces of the country and rank them in order of the amount of grain produced, the Hon. Member's home Province of Saskatchewan is the largest producer; Alberta is the second largest; Ontario is third, followed by Manitoba. The fact is that Ontario produces a large amount of grain and is very much affected by what the Hon. Member for Prince Alberta referred to as an extraordinary situation.
It is an extraordinary situation, and we face a very difficult market as a result of the Europeans and the Americans essentially engaging in a price war. In my view, it is largely brought on by the actions of the European community as a result of dramatically increasing agricultural production, especially in the grain sector, through some very large subsidies.
Let me point out that it is not in any way the strategy of this Government to eliminate farmers. I hesitate to even dignify that question with an answer. The Hon. Member should know very well that this Government supports agriculture. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said at a press conference some two weeks ago that: "there's more we have to do for western agriculture and we're going to try to do it within the constraints imposed upon us by this economic situation". That is certainly a refreshing attitude on the part of a Prime Minister of this country, not only on behalf of western agriculture but Canadian agriculture as a whole.
I believe that our record in terms of supporting agriculture, especially western agriculture, has been very good. In the calendar year 1985, the federal Government was responsible for close to $1.5 billion of new initiatives or ongoing initiatives in western Canada to support the grain industry. That is a significant amount of money, and it should indicate that the Government is very willing to support agriculture.
The Hon. Member heard the Prime Minister state in Question Period today that Canada intended to raise the agricultural trade issue at the Tokyo meeting. Again, that
Adjournment Debate
indicates this Government's support for Canadian agriculture. In anticipation of the Tokyo meeting, the Prime Minister will be meeting a group of farm representatives from across the country on Thursday to hear their concerns and let them know that we in fact are concerned about agriculture.
I believe that our record of support for agriculture is good. We want to maintain that record and do whatever we can to improve it so that Canadian farmers are not the casualties in this very severe price war between the European community and the United States.

subtopic: TRANSPORTATION OF DANGEROUS GOODS-REQUEST THAT LEGISLATION BE STRENGTHENED
TRANSPORTATION OF DANGEROUS GOODS-REQUEST THAT LEGISLATION BE STRENGTHENED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some time ago I asked the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankow-ski) about the status of legislation concerning the transportation of dangerous goods. He informed the House that broad regulations covering the transportation of dangerous goods were proclaimed on July 1, 1985. The regulations cover all modes of transportation; air, water, rail and road. Interprovincial transport by road was the only important mode of transportation not covered by these regulations because it is a provincial not federal jurisdiction. As of February of 1986, the provinces and the territories adopted similar legislation to cover transportation of dangerous goods by road and which enforced the transportation of dangerous goods regulations. The ultimate aim of the transportation of dangerous goods regulations is to create a set of uniform regulatory requirements which apply to all means of transportation.
The Act and regulations are an attempt to rationalize the transportation of dangerous goods across Canada. Dangerous goods such as toxic chemicals, highly flammable or explosive products, radioactive materials, corrosives and so on constitute a real threat to our communities when they are not transported safely. The Mississauga derailment in 1979, in which a train containing cars of chlorine gas derailed, resulted in a massive evacuation of the city of Mississauga for several days. Fortunately, no lives were lost during this emergency. However, there are certainly no guarantees that we will be so lucky again.
The mode of transportation, the type of container, and the labelling of materials are all important aspects which contribute to the safer transportation of dangerous goods. Another factor which is of great concern to many, including the Corporation of the City of Toronto and a group of concerned citizens called "M-TRAC", the Metro-Toronto Residents' Action Committee for Rail Safety, is the speed at which trains pass through densely populated urban areas.
In March of this year the City of Toronto submitted a brief to the Acting President of the Canadian Transport Commission and to the Chairman of the Railway Transport Committee requesting that train speeds be reduced to 25 miles per hour on the CP North Toronto subdivision line. The brief points out that in 1981, the Railway Transport Committee


Adjournment Debate
imposed a maximim speed limit of 35 miles per hour on trains carrying full loads of special dangerous goods. The city is still greatly concerned, however, about trains carrying partial loads or empty cars with residue of dangerous chemicals. Unless some further action is taken, the risks will continue to increase and so will the potential for disaster. The City of Toronto states in its brief, and I quote:
-some risks cannot be avoided in urban areas. The transport by rail of ever increasing loads of toxic and explosive chemicals through high density areas, where evacuation may be difficult if not impossible, imposes an unfair and unjustified risk to many residents of the city of Toronto. The time for action is now for we are just one accident from a disaster.
In its response to the position paper of the Minister of Transport, "Freedom to Move", M-TRAC expresses its concerns that deregulation may lead to laxity in safety. Certainly the proclamation of the transportation of dangerous goods regulations in July of 1985 has alleviated some concerns. However, M-TRAC is more particularly concerned for the people in highly congested urban areas who are especially vulnerable to train derailment and resultant spillage of dangerous cargo.
There are many people who are concerned about this important issue. Harry Behrend, Vice-Chairman of M-TRAC, and my friend, Rose Dyson, are two people who have been greatly concerned about and involved in making the issues of transporting dangerous goods by rail and the speed at which trains pass through heavily urbanized areas, priority concerns. Last summer, my colleague, the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway), my wife Sandy and I went on a fact-finding tour of the CP Rail main line through Toronto to learn more about the situation and the risks involved. CP Rail officials were helpful in answering our inquiries.
One of the ways in which the railways are attempting to make their mode of transportation safer is through the use of a new type of wheel bearing to improve performance and safety standards. I believe CP has converted something like 75 per cent of the bearings to date.
It should be noted, however, that dangerous goods are not transported just by rail, although this is certainly the mode of transport which has attracted the most attention. The use of other modes of transportation, such as by truck or tanker, is also prevalent. It is vital that the appropriate regulations be followed to the letter to ensure that dangerous goods are transported safely, with no threat to the surrounding population. This is an important issue which concerns Canadians, especially those who live in densely populated urban areas, such as my riding of Don Valley East.
On a positive note, a federal task force was set up on March 14, 1986, by the Minister of Transport to study the transportation of dangerous goods by rail in the Metropolitan Toronto area. On the task force are representatives of CN, CP, M-TRAC, and the public at large. While they have two years to
conduct their research and compile their recommendations, speed reduction has been identified as an urgent issue. I look forward to an interim report in this regard. I also look forward to their final recommendations on how to improve the safety factors, thereby protecting the public when dangerous goods are being transported through Metropolitan Toronto so that we never have anything close to the disaster which occurred in Mississauga in 1979.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. M. Forrestall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: TRANSPORTATION OF DANGEROUS GOODS-REQUEST THAT LEGISLATION BE STRENGTHENED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the Hon. Member for Don Valley East (Mr. Attewell) has dealt to a great extent with rail passenger traffic and the establishment of the task force, I will direct myself more particularly to his concerns regarding trucking.
At the outset, I would remind Hon. Members that regulations respecting the classification of dangerous goods, the documentation and marking of them, the preparation of emergency response plans, the reporting of spills, and, above all, the training of those responsible for the handling of dangerous goods, have already been promulgated. In fact, as the Hon. Member has mentioned, these measures have been in effect across the country since July 1, 1985.
By long-standing agreement with the provinces, they will have the primary role of enforcing the regulations with respect to vehicular traffic, that is, truck traffic, as it respects dangerous goods. Ontario has taken the lead among the provinces in the application of regulations. It has trained all of its highway inspectors and weigh scale operators and it has been working closely with the Ontario Trucking Association and a number of private trucking associations, not the least of which is the Ontario Petroleum Association, to ensure that vehicle operators are fully aware of the nature and hazards of the products they are transporting. The other provinces are conducting the same compliance programs. In fact, all provinces have been enforcing the regulations since February, 1986.
Discussions with a view to amending aspects of the legislation are presently under way which I hope will address, in part, the Hon. Member's concern. However, I must underline for the Hon. Member that this is only enabling legislation. It is the regulations which give teeth to the legislation. It is an awareness program. It is in education that we will achieve safety, not through legislation or regulation alone. Education is equally important.
